utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, The Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, everybody. Thank you. All the accused are here. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Defence, I notice the absence of Ms. Tapuskovic, Mr. Bourgon, and Mr. Haynes. Dobar dan gospodine, Professor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Hopefully we will finish with your testimony very soon, and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope so too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You've been extremely helpful and very cooperative. I didn't expect your testimony to last this long, so I'm sorry if it did. But it means that the parties have attached, obviously, a lot of importance to it. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And good morning to you Mr. Remetic. I going to try and -- well, I will comply with the Trial Chamber's direction, but I'm going to try myself to move this along. Now, yesterday, you talked about certain words that were particular to the Dalmatian coast. One of the words was the word "sjor;" is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And the word "sjor" is derivative or related to the word "Signor," right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Signor. A Romanesque term.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the context of your observation of Mr. Beara, his speech in April of this year, the use of that term corresponds with the dialect that you heard him use when you interviewed him?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in fact, that dialect incorporates other Romanisms as well?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what specific words you are referring to. Surely not only in the Cakavian but in all other coastal regions, even deep into the territory of Montenegro are full of Romanisms. The area of Mount Durmitor, the area from which Vuk Karadzic originated, is full of Romanisms. Even the name Durmitor is derived from Latin.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm only referring to the dialect that you observed Mr. Beara use. That's all. Does that incorporate other Romanisms other than the word "sjor"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the term "skape"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the term "skape." You can find them on Mount Durmitor as well. These are openings in rocks, pits, holes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is the use of that term consistent with the dialect that you heard Mr. Beara use in April of this year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I don't know about this detail, but I do not rule out the possibility, just as it is probable to hear the word "skape" even out side the Cakavian-speaking regions. You can also here them in the Stokavian-speaking regions. It is not marked. It is a wide-spread word equal to the use of the word "burazer."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So there's nothing linguistically distinctive about the use of that word in your opinion; is that right? You can answer yes or no so we can move this along.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because half of the words have been borrowed from other languages. The word "soba" comes from the word Hungarian. "Carapa" comes from Turkish. Half of the garments that I have on me do not have Slavic origins in their names. And let me remind you of something if you allow me, and it is my duty to do so, and I beg for your patience. Since we are insistent on individual cases, this whole region experienced turbulent history. Various civilisations and administrations existed there and left their traces behind. The region where Beara and I spent our youth, that is Bosnia and Herzegovina, had been part of Austria-Hungaria for 40 years. People joined the army under the German command, and I can ascertain -- and I'm speaking from my experience that illiteral people were eager and are still eager to use in Bosnia various words that they learned from the commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. My question is really quite limited and specific, and that is whether or not the word "skape" carries linguistic significance in your opinion, and you can tell me yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It has a linguistic significance. It is a Romanism in our dialect. It is not marked either territorially or dialectically. It is widespread.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, yesterday we talked a little bit - or maybe a lot, actually - about language or dialect as an identifiable feature that is mutable. We talked about the concept of code-shifting, which is changing dialects, and we also talked about changing dialects in the context of somebody that is bidialectal, that they can speak two different dialects or understand two different dialects.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You observed in your report, if you recall, on page 14 that Mr. Beara was without fault when translating all detailed differences and constructions from the texts attributed to him into his linguistic model. That's in your report at page 14, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, are you aware of any studies that relate to the effects of switching dialects, that is on the listener?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's common knowledge. These issues have been the subject of numerous dialectological studies. I did not especially address this issue. My area of study was the influence of other dialects on their neighbouring dialects, for which purpose Bosnia is a particularly good ground since it has three religions, and religious affiliation as a rule is reflected in the differences in dialects. On the 3rd of March of this year, I held an academic speech on the subject of the Serbian dialects of Bosnia in the light of dialectical interference and its linguistic and social linguistic aspect. I viewed this topic in a broader framework in order to find out to what extent the Bosniaks and the Croats have influence with their dialect, that of the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. What I wanted to know specifically was whether you were acquainted with a study that was conducted in Sweden. In particular, it derives from a article that is entitled "Switch Of Dialect As Disguise," and it is written by Sjostrom, Eriksson, Zetterholm, Sullivan, and published in 2006, part of the centre of languages and literature department in university there. And in particular what they caution is that because a dialect can be switched or imitated, that "forensic practitioners who currently use dialect as a primary feature during analysis need to reduce their reliance on this feature and be aware that they can be easily misled." Are you familiar with such a concept, and is that something that you took into consideration when you interviewed Mr. Beara in April of this year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not wrong, that implies that someone is willingly changing his dialect. Are you referring to that, that someone is willingly and knowingly switching to another dialect in order to conceal his identity? If this is what you mean, well, these problems are beyond my scope of expertise, and I don't see any reason for this being done. I'm not an expert in these kind of issues. You can call it a disguise, and when you say "disguise," it, I assume, implies a willing act or a knowing act, and I didn't see any purpose for that, for that kind of behaviour on the part of Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you about the circumstances under which you examined him, then. When you went to go visit Mr. Beara at the detention unit - I think you testified to - first, that was an appointment; he was expecting you. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a meeting had been convened.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He knew that you were coming there for the specific purpose of evaluating his speech, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I wished to meet him to have a talk with him and to see and hear in what way he is talking now. It goes without saying that if he is going to be visited by a linguist, then, sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is correct that he knew you were coming there for the specific purpose of evaluating his speech? That's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is also correct that he knew that you were there for the specific purpose of evaluating his speech in the context of these specific intercepts. That's true too, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. All I know is that I saw and heard that he definitely still speaks in the way that he spoke at the beginning of the war and as he was identified by his fellow combatants from the Army of Republika Srpska when they thought that he was a Croat. I said on several occasions the Beara of pre-war period speaks Cakavian, Ikavian, and Croatian, and he still speaks that. There is something else, however, in the transcripts, and this is the problem that I faced, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Having conducted that interview, did you determine whether or not Mr. Beara had access to the intercepts against which you were going to compare his dialect? You can answer that yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. No, no, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did you inquire as to whether or not he had access to the information against which you were going to compare your observations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So you never asked him whether or not he'd seen the intercepts that you were there to compare his speech against?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You never asked his attorney. Whether his attorney provided him with those intercepts that you were going to compare your observations against?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember asking him that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Today, as you testify in court, you have absolutely no ability to say whether or not Mr. Beara was familiar with the intercepts that you were comparing his voice against and is the subjects of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are asking me if I knew whether he knew. I don't know. I don't know if he knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Remetic, isn't a relevant consideration to know whether or not Mr. Beara has knowledge of the intercepts in question since you are comparing what he is telling you against what you're observing in those documents? Isn't that an important thing to know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in my view, the important thing was first to sit on the side and listen to him talking to other persons, then to talk to him on specific topics, and then I was assured that I could use this procedure on the basis on a number of examples that I had on paper from the transcript. And I asked him a question to which he replied to me, this is the way the Serbian people speak, this is the way the Montenegrins speak; and this is as a linguist is the path that I took, and I wouldn't have done it any differently if I had to do it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you interviewed Mr. Beara, you observed his speech in the context of his discussions with his lawyers, right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You observed that speech on the 7th of April in the context of his discussions with Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Meek in the presence of Ms. Dzambazovic, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And you observed that speech also in the context of his discussions with Mr. Ostojic and the presence of Ms. Dzambazovic on the following day, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You directly posed questions to Mr. Beara in order to determine distinctions that he can make relevant to the purpose of your examination of these intercepts, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in the context of what information he gave you, you compared these intercepts against the way he presented himself over that 7- or 8-hour period of observation, right? You can answer that just yes or --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You testified previously that putting direct questions to the subject of an analysis during a linguistic examination of that person is something that is not in accordance with the canons of your profession?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but when you examine an illiterate person who speaks in a certain dialect is quite a different thing. I made a clear distinction that in this particular case I was able to do that because I was dealing with a very intelligent and cooperative collocutor, and let me tell, you there were not too many questions of that kind because what I heard on the first day was enough for me to create a clear picture of the way that Beara speaks nowadays. As for my conclusions on the transcripts I reached them within the context not only of his present dialect because as I said so many times before, not to discard that altogether in advance, but I, rather, looked at the standard Croatian language that he uses outside the dialect itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The reason why a linguist doesn't put direct questions on dialect to the subject of his examination is because he can influence the results. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are absolutely right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That has nothing to do with the literacy, Mr. Remetic. It has nothing to do with literacy; that's true, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, until April this year I researched the dialect only through conversations with authentic speakers who were born in the certain region and very poorly literate or totally illiterate. This method by posing questions I applied only after I had a clear picture of the present linguistic model employed by Mr. Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And in determining that linguistic model by Mr. Beara, you didn't consider his possible motivation to be less than candid with you about the way he speaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for interrupting, and I do have to object. I think we've heard enough of this. If the Prosecution has evidence that Mr. Beara changed or altered his dialect, they should bring it forth. This is purely speculation. It's something that I know they utilize in their cross, but there's no evidence that he changed or altered his speech at any time. But they should have concrete evidence and put it to the witness, or perhaps they should bring their linguist, which they don't have, to share with us these concepts that my learned friend is learning from the literature or reading from the literature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think you have misread Mr. Vanderpuye's question. It's a very simple question, and it's a straightforward one, whether in his assessment the gentleman, professor, considered or not the possible motivation on the part of accused Beara to mislead the professor in the course of his work. So please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no reason to suspect because I realized and I was almost shocked and surprised to such an extent that he still speaks in the same manner that he spoke before the war, that he is using the Split-based Cakavian dialect as I had been told. I was surprised. Anyway, gentlemen, Mr. Beara is here, and any other approach in this analysis is possible. We have the subject, the speaker, and my findings can be cross-checked, and it can be verified whether he is still speaking the same way as he did before as I stated, and I think this should be much easier for you to do that then for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Remetic, the logic in which you assessed --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- subsumes that you've made the determination already, preconceived determination of how Mr. Beara spoke before you spoke to him, because what you've said is you had a linguistic model about how he spoke before the war in order to analyse how he spoke during the war by comparing it against what you observed after the war. That's the whole purpose of your determination is to figure out how he spoke during the war. That's the subject of the intercept, isn't it, Mr. Remetic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I had three assignments or three things to do. I'm begging your pardon sir, please. Actually, I had three things. I had transcripts, I had an insight into how Beara speaks today, and I had information that early he spoke as a Croat would do. He was in service in Split. I could only assume what standard he used, and I was surprised and never expected that I would encounter this speech model as I did in the detention unit. I was surprised. I was astonished, sir, and I said yesterday that if I had been 30 years younger or if I were 30 years younger now, if I were just starting my career, I would analyse his speech pattern very seriously. I did not come to confirm anything. I just wanted to see how his -- or hear, rather, how he speaks today. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you met with Mr. Beara -- or rather, let me withdraw that and rephrase it. Your comparison is based only on examination of what he -- your examination of the intercepts is based only upon a comparison against what he sounded like in 2008 when you met him, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did most of the work before meeting with Beara. So I returned home on the 9th, and already on the 18th I dispatched my final report. I had been working on it for months. It's logical, it can be verified, and this is something that goes without saying, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. So you didn't consider any other speech, a known speech attributable to Mr. Beara at any time before 2008?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I've already said that on several occasions. I expected to find traces of his childhood, but I didn't find anything, nothing that would be differential, nothing that would be marked. And let me repeat once again; later on, I practically excluded the speeches of northwestern Serbia when he doesn't speak Ikavian. He speaks Croatian just like my host he is who said to me yesterday, let's go "lijevo," left, just like Beara said when he addressed the lady and told her why are you so pale, "blijeda." I understand that fully. This is Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that. My question is whether -- a very simple question, and I understand that your answer is in fact you did not consider any other speech known to be attributed to Mr. Beara before 2008. Yes, that's correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who is it who attributes speech to him, and what speech is attributed to him? Nobody attributes anything to him. I was just told that he spoke Croatian, that he spoke Croatian as any Croatian would do, so I just assumed that he would be using the Split variant of the Cakavian dialect. What speech are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me give you an example. Were you made aware of an article that was published in Svedok, 29 October 2002? Were you made aware of an article attributing certain statements to Mr. Beara by his attorneys, by Mr. Beara, or by anyone else?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, no. No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Any information concerning a statement or some exemplar of Mr. Beara's speech from Mr. Beara, his attorneys, his wife, or any other source?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't. The only thing I requested were audiotapes of the intercepts, and attorneys told me that they did not have any because the only thing I was asked to do was to analyse that material.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ostojic went over a number of intercepts that you reviewed. I'd like to draw your attention to a couple of them, if I may. What I'd like to draw your attention to is 65 ter 3627. If I could have that on the -- in e-court, please. If I could, please, may we go to the page with the ERN number ending 153, 7153. All right. Okay. If we could just go to the -- if you could just look at the fourth line from the bottom of that page. All right. It would be the top line now on the page. That's attributable to Mr. Beara. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where? What text? There are several sentences here containing the word "Beara."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, I'm talking about the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which text? Which sentence? Give me the beginning of the sentence. There's several of them here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Go up two lines. That may help you. Okay. The first one starts with -- looks like "Znas sta." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And in particular, I'm referring to the part where it says "etencina bre."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, what type of language is that? What type of dialect is that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This form may originate in two ways. It could to be Ikavian, and in the Croatian variant "prijek" could be "prek" [phoen] because R is dropped out after J like "brijeg" and plural is "bregovi," as in "lijevobi" [phoen] becomes "ljevo" or -- and this "prek" can be the original Ikavian or it could be a derivative of the Croatian "prijek." This form is not a reliable identifier. It is not well marked for anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Is it consistent with the dialect that you observed Mr. Beara -- that Mr. Beara spoke to you with in April of this year?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not Ikavian but it could be the Croatian variants of the former common language or what is currently known as the Croatian language. In the Croatian the form is "prijek" and the derivative is "prek." This is not part of the dialect that he uses, but it could be part of the standard language that he uses.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. What about two lines down, you see a word attributed to Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Which on the tape appears to be "kretencina bre." Now, is that something --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- that is consistent in the dialect of Mr. Beara?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This "bre," I don't think so. "Bre" is something that is a filler word, primarily in Serbia, and this is also something that could have creeped into the language of the officers because the officers of the army hale from all over the place. This is not imminent to the coastal Cakavian linguistic area. It is more commonly heard in the eastern parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And he hales from there but spent a substantial amount of time in the western part, which he demonstrated to you when you interviewed him, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to Intercept 3607. Before we do, by the way, on 3627, the one that's on the screen, you did reach the determination that is Mr. Beara on the tape, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is Beara.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's go to 3607, please. All right. If we could we could go to page with ERN ending 7108. All right. I think it's all right if Mr. Remetic can see that. At the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You see the term "Gdje," G-d-j-e with a question mark attributed to Mr. Beara. Do you see that, Mr. Remetic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure that I heard him say "gdje." I'm not sure that I heard him that way. The recording was not that clear to me. I know that this is part of the standard norm, however, in practice; and this is something that I stated in my statement in free-flow communication. The way people speak in Bosnia is different. They will say "Je." That's in Bosnian. That's also how I would speak in communication with my relatives and colleagues who are Bosniaks and Croats and who are also linguists from Sarajevo, but this would be in free communication when I talk to them on the phone. I would never use it in a paper, or I would never use it speaking from a rostrum.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. In your report on page 16, you say that Mr. Beara today says "gdi", g-d-i, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Gdi" is what he says most of the time. However, if he uses the standard form, then it can be "di" or "gdi". I've told you that there's no single village, either Cakavian or Stokavian, that would be purely linguistically defined, and this, of course, applies even more to any educated man who is well versed in speaking a standard norm.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Remetic, if it's not linguistically defined, then it has no linguistic significance in terms of making identification, right, particular in individual identification?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you know -- what do you mean? Are you referring just to this form, or are you referring to the whole body of the analysed text?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm referring to is sub (a) in section 11 of your report where you specifically point out that Mr. Beara's "current manner of speech is in sharp contrast to these facts," referring to the term "gde," g-d-e, and you say that Mr. Beara today says "gde" as a significant linguistic distinction, which you are now apparently contradicting. That's what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not contradicting anything. I adhered to what I said about Beara's speech, and I based that on the eight hours of my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. With respect to this intercept, 3607, you had an opportunity to hear that. Is that Mr. Beara's voice on this intercept?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression is that it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me refer you, then, to intercept 3626. If we could have that in e-court, please. Okay. All right, in this intercept, if you go, well, first of all to the third line from the bottom or the fourth line from the bottom, you see the term "los muchachos," right, that I'd referred to yesterday. Do you see that, Mr. Remetic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Now, if we could go down a little bit on this page. All right. The second to last line on the page in front of you now, you see the word "gde," g-d-e, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's not -- okay. If you go -- now, are we on the next page on this? If we could go down a little bit or to the next page if there's nothing. You see the line that begins "kako nisi." You see that? It's the third line down on this page.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this you see, again, the term g-d-e," gde," right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. You heard this tape, as well, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And this was a tape also of Mr. Beara, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me take you to Intercept 65 -- well it's intercept, 13 July 1995, at 1009, and that is 65 ter 1130. I don't think I need it in e-court, but let me ask you first. This is an intercept that contains language to the effect of Sjor Lucic, which is attributed to Mr. Beara. Do you remember this intercept, or shall I put it on the screen for you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first intercept, sir, with Sjor Lucic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. And "sjor" you've indicated is a typically Dalmatian term?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yet in your report you conclude that the dialect does not reveal the speaker's origin, and you reason in your report that that's because it doesn't appear in the other intercept that you evaluated.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the swallow, remember. That one swallow was what initiated the search for a flock, and there was no flock.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You also point out in that intercept -- in your analysis of that intercept is the use of the term "gde." That's on page 16 of your report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That was the basis for excluding Mr. Beara as a potential participant in this conversation in your analysis?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this was not the basis. If you have looked at my report very carefully, you will remember that I say in it that the language is not marked for variances, that in every text there are elements of both the western and eastern variants of the common language and that the western variant prevails. Please, I'm reminding you that this is what I say in my report, and I have also stated in my report that there are more Ijekavian forms and only one "gde." "Sjor" was something that would be marked, but there was just one confirmation that never repeated again. In everyday language, this word shares the status of "burazer," and there are quite a few of the word "burazer" in there. I drew my conclusions based on the relationship between the western and eastern variant characteristics. The intercept that contains "los muchachos" and "dogadja" is the intercept that I would attribute to Beara's name, not because of the "los muchachos" as much as for "dogadja," but then when you have both "los muchachos" and "dogadja," you draw conclusions based on that. Not a single transcript is very well marked for variants. Wherever there is text, there are both groups of forms, so there's no single transcript that can be attributed exclusively to either the western or the eastern model, and there is practically no Cakavian dialect in any of them except for this word "sjor" in one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. But you do have this word "sjor" in one of them, and despite that word "sjor" being in one of them, you conclude that you don't have enough information to attribute this intercept to Mr. Beara, which conversely means you don't have enough information to exclude Mr. Beara doesn't it, Mr. Remetic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I didn't have them then, and I don't have them now, either.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. If we could, we can go to intercept 15 July. Let's start with 15 July, 094 hours, 65 ter 1178. All right. This is an intercept that you mentioned in your report as I have it on page 18. Now, in this report you conclude that it's not possible to accept without reservation the view that this relates to Mr. Beara who did not explicitly identify himself as such, even the - I can't even say this word - hypochoristic Ljubo does not appear; and in any case, it could refer to the bearers [Realtime transcript read in error, "Bearas"] of some 30 names, right? You then say, hereto appears the noun "burazer," which accompanies the majority of the text initially connected with Ljubisa Beara. Okay. Now, you've already said that "burazer" has no linguistic significance because it's used everywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, my learned friend. On page 19, line 21, I think that report actually uses the word "bearer" with a small B and not the name "Beara" as I think they typed, just so the record's is clear on that, and I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I think you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sorry. I'm not sure what he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I just -- the error.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: On the report -- you simply -- on the report, you read it I think correctly, but I think it was just transcribed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's a question of transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Oh, all right. I'm sorry. I missed it. Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Vanderpuye kindly be asked to speak up or closer to his microphone, please, for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'll do that, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, when you say that it's not possible to accept without reservation the view that this relates to Mr. Beara, it means you can't exclude him based on what you've seen in this intercept, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have no basis for establishing a link to Beara either in linguistic terms, and there's also one illogical aspect which is probably beyond the borders of linguistics, but it falls into the remain of some basic logics. And that is that a staff officer does not know where the 385 switchboard is. Further on, look at this: This transcript begins with 0954 and the next one, allegedly a minute later, and a test demonstrated that this alleged conversation lasted for 2 and a half minutes. And another thing: When you said that the word "burazer" was not a linguistic fact, I would say that everything is a linguistic fact. Even if I say "a" or "a," these are linguistic facts. However, there is a hierarchy of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's what I mean when I say "significant," but let me ask you this: Were you ever provided with any information that a participant in this conversation made a statement admitting his participation in this conversation with Mr. Beara? Were you ever made aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You weren't made aware of the fact that General Zivanovic, the Zivanovic mentioned in this intercept, made a statement on 2nd July, 2001, in an interview specifically saying that he recalled this conversation or that he made a statement in October of 2001 in which he says that he didn't want to get in trouble on the basis of one nebulous conversation between he and Beara, referring to this intercept?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I find Zivanovic interesting because the operator said that he remembered him as a person who is dropping his vocals, his vowels, and that means that his dialect is different, and that is the feature that he remembered Zivanovic by.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I ask because you attach a factual significance to this intercept in evaluating it rather than a linguistic one as concerns the reference to the extension 385. Do you know what the extension 385 corresponded to at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know why it is that Mr. Beara is asking for the switchboard? Which switchboard?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I served in the army from 1971 to 1972, and that is all of the experience that I have. I have no other knowledge, and I'm completely uninformed when it comes to the issues of that nature. And I can ascertain that I don't know anything about that, and I'm telling the truth and only the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you see in the intercept that General Zivanovic is essentially deferring this matter, indicating that he is not in a position to accommodate Mr. Beara. He says, I can't do that anymore, and then he says Zlatar and 385, call there. You recognise that in the intercept, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, we are going beyond the area of linguistics. I can only do some guesswork about this. Please, I am to -- nearing the end of my scientific career. The whereabouts of Zlatar and Badem, what is important to me was that Badem was adjusted. For me, it is important that the transcript and manuscript collate and the current speech used by Mr. Beara. However, these are the questions that I am not competent to give you answers to.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm asking you this because you have a number of other factual observations that you make that appear to be well beyond the scope of linguistics in your report, so let me refer you to the next one, and forgive me if I go a little bit out of order, but with respect to the intercept on 14 July 1995, you make a factual assessment of the intercept. On page 18 of your report, you say here the operator has unquestionably mixed up the speakers, and you base this on the fact that there are a number of -- it was a one-sided conversation that precedes the intercept. If I could put this up in e-court so everybody could see that. That's 1164. A is the English, and B is the -- should be E.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Mr. Vanderpuye is still a bit far from the microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I hope that's bit better.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What I'm referring to is right at the beginning. You see the letter "J," and it says hello. All right? You see this is "ko je major." You see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to this one: "Hello, Badem, put Beara on," and then, "who wants to speak to him"? Is that what you are referring to? "Hello. Who is the major? I'm the duty officer at Palma. I need Beara urgently." Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's what I'm referring to. Tell us what it is in this intercept that shows that the operator's apparently mixed up, and that's included in your report. What did you observe?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Further down you see B saying, "wait a little, old man."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you recognise in this report what it is you identify as the operator being mixed up? That's all my question is, and if you could point that out to us, that would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says, "Wait a moment. Just a moment, old man..." and this is uttered by someone called B, somewhere in the middle of the page. But at the very end they say that they intercepted the conversation by a mistake. They admitted a mistake in the procedure, but the words attributed to Mr. Beara in this text, because you can see that he was inaudible, this is so very little to go on. Why 155, where is that, and then again I'm asking myself a question, how is it possible that he doesn't know that location if he is the participant of some ...

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. You evaluated that in your linguistic capacity. Is that your testimony, Mr. Remetic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, this was just done en passant because the part -- there's no part of the text that can be attributed to Beara. It doesn't offer any data for an analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because allegedly it was impossible to hear him as we can see from these dots in the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that, Mr. Remetic. If I could refer you to 65 ter 1179. This is the intercept of 15 July 1995 at 957. Do you recall this intercept, sir, or do you want me to put it on the screen for you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I do not need the screen. It's the issue of whether it was one or three conversations. After a lengthy and thorough analysis, I concluded that there was one conversation that was subsequently adjusted and harmonised, and I explained that in great detail, the discrepancies, the chronology of the beginning, 55, 57, 1000.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, you are unaware, then, that these intercepts - that is, 955, 957 and 1000 - were captured by three different interceptors? You are either aware or you're not; can you tell us which?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It might be that there were three persons, and I elaborated on this issue accurately, and I tried to find justification for chronological discrepancies, whether their watches were not working properly and were not set to match each other. They probably did not establish connections at the same time. According to their statements, they were working under difficult conditions; and thirdly, it is possible that you cannot hear the person all the time so that you have blank spaces. I allow for all these possibilities, sir, and it makes sense. However, where they match, one can see evident differences. The beginning is different. The identification of the speakers is substantially different. Let me remind you, in the first version at 0955, Mr. Beara explicitly introduced himself with his full name by saying Ljubo Beara. The next version say that is he introduced himself allegedly as Colonel Beara, whereas in the third version there is no introduction by name. Please. And then the very linguistic content and the variance, you had an opportunity to see the table differs. If you hear the same thing from three sources, how come that you make different notes? These are very serious discrepancies, and they are of fundamental importance for this assignment. The very few facts that we had at our disposal made our task very difficult and complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Remetic, what you're talking about right now are factual questions as distinct from the linguistic analysis that you were retained to conduct, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I see it, the crucial thing is whether a person introduces himself or not. This is what I wrote in the preamble of my report. I took that into consideration, sir. The analysis was carried out. You have it in front of you. You have the tables and comparisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, did you take into consideration this, that the fact is that Mr. Beara on a tape that you heard actually did introduce himself loud and clear in a way that you could identify his voice independently of his name and the fact that he did use his name, and that is in 3603? It's a tape that you heard and talked about in your direct examination by Mr. Ostojic. It is -- did you take that into consideration?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question. I do apologise. Can you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In the intercept at 0955 hours, 65 ter 1179, there's an attribution to Mr. Beara apparently saying "Ljubo Beara." In the intercept at 3603, there's an attribution to Mr. Beara in which he says "Ljubo Beara." In other words, he introduced himself on that intercept as well.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about what is written in the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As am I. And I am asking --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear -- this is what is written in the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm asking whether as a linguist in trying to determine whether or not it is possible that the intercept involves Mr. Beara you considered such facts as that he introduced himself on another intercept using both his first and last name as it appears in an intercept which you didn't have a tape for that you examined. Did you consider that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but how can you have three different forms in the same conversation? That's the problem. He may say, this is Beara, this is Ljubo, this is Colonel Beara. It's all possible, but we have here one conversation recorded by three operators, and each of them did that or conveyed that differently. From a linguistic point of view, I find that to be strange. If we have a single conversation, then either they put dots where there are blank spaces, probably they didn't here, but if they heard the conversation, how is it possible that they heard different things? If you can provide an explanation to me for that, I would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm glad that you asked the question, and what I'd like to know is whether or not you asked to see the testimony of these particular individuals before you wrote your report or at any time after to search for that answer. Did you ask Mr. Ostojic for the testimony of these particular operators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't ask for their testimonies. I don't even know whether that was necessary or permissible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You're saying you want to know why it is the case, and you're telling us that you never asked why? You never asked for their testimony - is that fair to say - to review their explanation of how that's the case?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, are we talking about the statements or testimonies given by the operators? You corrected me yesterday. I did read the statements (redacted). Please, the statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we could go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: When you evaluated these particular intercepts - that is, 955, 957 and 10 o'clock intercepts - there's also, well, a confluence of certain information in those intercepts, isn't there? That is, one intercept you see a reference to a person by the name of Furtula; in another intercept, you see the reference to the name of Burtula; and yet in another, you see a reference to the name of Furtula, right? You see the reference to the name of Nasic in one and Nastic in another?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So there's a certain -- okay. And there's a certain degree of confluence in the information that's contained in those intercepts. Even as a layperson, you can see that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Two persons hear things differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if I could just refer you to the August 1st, 2245 intercept, and you've put that together, also, with the August 1st, 2308 intercept. Those are 65 ter 1380 and 1381 respectively. With respect to those intercepts, according to your chart Mr. Beara is not revealed, the language does not -- the dialect, rather, doesn't reflect his -- the speaker's origin, et cetera. You have negatives for all fields. Bear with me for one moment. On the August 1st intercept, 2245, that is the intercept in which the term "skape" is used or "skape" is used. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: According to you, that has no linguistic significance, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if we do not understand each other. Every fact has a certain linguistic significance. In my hotel room, I have a monography on the subject of onomastics of Piva, the River Piva, where skape is mentioned on several occasions. I told you that the toponym term "skape" says that, for instance, there are dozens of skape in the area of Durmitor. Therefore, it is not marked; it is not limited; it is widespread and "skape" appears in many Ekavian forms. This here is a medley, and I marked the 1st of August as a mixture of various hardly compatible types of dialects and standard forms of the language.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And unfortunately, we do not have the manuscript.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. That intercept talks about prisoners captured in Serbia - that is the intercept at 65 ter 1380, 2245 - as does the intercept at 65 ter 1381 discuss similar issues. Were you made aware that an intercept dated 2nd August at 1300 hours was captured on tape and played in this proceeding?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned about that, I guess, over the weekend.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you aware -- sorry, are you aware that that particular intercept refers to Mr. Beara as having called a person identified as Popovic on the tape?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Which intercept on the tape? I apologise. Are you talking about the first August intercept? I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The 2nd August, 1300 hours, was captured on tape and played in this proceeding. That intercept --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear that, no. Please, no, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That particular intercept --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, this conversation has nothing whatsoever to do from my point of view with Mr. Beara. 2nd of August at 1300 hours is absolutely irrelevant for me. Beara is mentioned in it, but I did not -- I don't see his words. The words that he himself uttered, sir, are not at 1300 hours, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. What I'm talking about in terms of relevance --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I think I can finish in 5 minutes or 10 minutes with the Court's permission. I know that I'm over my allotted time as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. We did give an allowance to Mr. Ostojic, and we can't not give some extra time to you. However, it's break time, and I think we could have the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We could have the break now. In any case, there's going to be a re-examination, so I think we better give the witness a little bit of respite now. 25 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. -- Recess taken at 10.31 a.m. -- On resuming at 11.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. Remetic, I have only a couple of questions for you, and then I think we're done. Now, with respect to what I was just referring to at 65 ter 1395, 2nd August, 1300, intercept, I'm sure you know it's the Prosecution's position that this intercept is related to the previous two intercepts on the preceding day in that it involves Mr. Beara on its face and relates to issues involving prisoners in Serbia. Is it your position that this conversation on August 2nd at 1300 is not of any relevance to you given the fact that it's on tape and refers to Mr. Beara and his involvement with these individuals in Serbia in terms of identifying Mr. Beara as a potential participant in the prior two conversations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the point of view of a linguist and from the point of view of the assignment given to me as a linguist, this conversation is absolutely irrelevant. In this alleged intercept, there are no words uttered by Mr. Beara. My assignment was to state whether based on the language in the 18 intercept, these intercepts may be attributed to Mr. Beara. In this particular intercept, Mr. Beara is speaking. He is not there, and as far as your perspective is concerned, things may be viewed differently, but that's beyond the scope of my task, beyond the scope of my interest. I don't even remember what the OTP says. I only say those intercepts where it is stated this is Ljubo, the other Ljubo, or we are not sure which Ljubo is concerned here. That's how I understood my task.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. And with respect to your analysis of the intercepts that are attributed by the Prosecution to Mr. Beara, it is true as you stated in your report that the absence of tape recordings of these conversations makes it practically -- well, practically prevents you or any other expert in your place from rising above pure hypothesis. That's on page 16 of your report. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are cases, of course, where there is not enough elements to arrive at any firm conclusions. The absence of any recordings is a handicap of sorts; for example, looking at the 2nd August intercept that I also heard on an audiotape, and not even the OTP was certain who the tape could be attributed to, I can say that it may be attributed to Mr. Beara. And I repeat, the absence of the audiotapes is a huge handicap in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Remetic, if you bear with me and I'll just locate this in the text. On page 16 of your report you say, I'll just quote it: "The likelihood that an analysed text may be attributed to Mr. Ljubisa Beara will depend on the type of responses to the above questions. In all this, one must bear in mind the fact that this expert witness was not provided with audio recordings of the alleged conversations that are part of my analysis" -- "part of this analysis" - I'm sorry - "which practically prevents him and any other expert in his place from rising above pure hypothesis and positively identifying Ljubisa Beara as a participant in the conversations attributed to him." That's what is in your report, and that is true, right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Remetic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President and Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye, and thank you, Witness. Mr. Ostojic. You have re-examination, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Remetic, if I can just start, perhaps, where my learned friend left off. How did you think -- or did you find in analysing the documents that the Prosecution provided for us, do you have any idea how they came up with their criteria for determining which Ljubo is -- should be attributed to which person? Did they ever give us that information, do you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think it calls for speculation. It's completely inappropriately put to this witness as to what the Prosecution -- how the Prosecution came up with its interpretation of the intercepts.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think my learned friend misunderstood my question. I'm not asking him to speculate. I'm asking, did they provide us any analysis or any information as to how they came up with their purported analysis, speculative or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If that's the case, then it's a question of relevance, as well, and it's objectionable because it's completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, I totally disagree. I think it is relevant since they carry the burden of proof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We consider it a valid question. However, you just please restrict yourself in answering the question to whether you know or not, okay? That's how I understood the question, and that's how it can be put and answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only thing that comes to mind is that the OTP started from the operators' allegations. In some of the transcripts, the operators identify the participants by giving their names. In some other transcripts, on the other hand, the participants identify either themselves personally or each other. Where no such procedure exists, I as a layperson in military terms would not be able to tell you how the intercepts and the participants in the conversations were identified or how the participants in certain conversations were linked with certain events.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Remetic. But really, I'm asking you with respect to where there was not a compromise of an identity by either the speaker -- either one of the speakers, when there's the name just "Ljubo," did you review any documents or anything that would show how the Prosecution came up with their analysis as to who that "Ljubo" should be -- or that conversation should be attributed to? Did you have any of that information? From, let's say, their linguist.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me go on to this issue: How many intercepts of the 18 did you review that had multiple purported conversations that were captured by different operators except for those that we've seen on the 15th of July at 955, 957 and 1000? utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conversation that took place on the 15th was transcribed by three different persons, and that's the only explanation I can provide. There are some other cases where there are two different versions, the first one usually crossed out and the second one valid, and then the last -- or the valid one was usually typed up on a typewriter. If my memory serves me well, and it does, the first intercept also has two versions, two different beginnings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, Professor, so we're talking about the intercept -- or you're talking about the intercept on the 13th of July 1995 at 1009, which is 65 ter 1130, which had in the beginning portion the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- manuscript and then rewritten after that. Are any others -- are there any other manuscripts, not the typed version. We know the process that some were typed, some were not, some had the manuscript, some didn't, and you've told us about that, and thank you very much for that. But I'm asking you of the 18 -- or of any of the intercepts that you reviewed, were there more than one intercept operator who captured a conversation except for that one on the 15th of July at the time that we said, 955, 957 and 1000?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you just a yes or no answer. However, in the notebook that I'm holding in my hand, there are several instances of one version being crossed out and the other typed up. I always analysed the typed-up version as well as the manuscript, which served as the template for the typed-up version. I did not pay much attention to the ones that were rejected in the process. Obviously, on the 15th of July was something that raised a big dilemma as to whether this was just one conversation or three different conversations or just one typed by three different persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Let me just move away and focus on whether or not you were fair and objective when you looked at these intercepts, and if we could have 2D551, please, and what we need -- that's his report, and what we need is appendix 1 just on the screen, if possible. Now, Mr. Remetic, I think the Court would permit you to look at your only table if you have it in front of you. It might be easier for you, so if you don't mind, if you could grab appendix 1, which is the overview of the results of the linguistic analysis that you provided. Take a look at it here.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We have now both of them there. I want to walk you through a couple of them just to see. When you give the designation zero, you're telling us in essence that, you know, you're not certain or it's insufficient information, correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no solid basis for any serious analysis or for any valid conclusions that would arise from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, I want to look at the one at the 23rd of July at 8 -- 0805 hours. I know you're called here as a witness in order to give us your objective opinion, but the Prosecution in that intercept themselves concede that it's not Mr. Beara, and they're saying it's some other Ljubo, actually Ljubo Bojanovic. How come you don't put a negative sign there, sir? Why did you keep it as insufficient? Did you just look at the corpus of the linguistic text that you had, and you didn't adopt what the Prosecution said or any attorneys, but you did it independent of what they thought and you left it as a zero, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It's obviously a leading question, Your Honour. I'd ask my friend to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, wait, wait, wait, Professor, because it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait, Professor. Wait. You either rephrase your question, or you move to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When we look at the 23rd of July, 1995, intercept, you know that -- what the Prosecution's position is in connection with that intercept, that the Ljubo mentioned in that intercept is a Ljubo Bojanovic. At 0805, having known that, can you just tell us why you placed a zero under the four categories in your table on appendix 1, please?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, this table, if I remember it well, was completed, or rather, the job was completed before I came aware of the OTP analysis. I've already said it here, that I completed most of the work before I ever met with Mr. Beara and spoke to him. Maybe. I believe that this is good, that this is better. If I met with Beara earlier, maybe November, I suppose -- or I believe that the report would be shorter because I would be less tempted to find different starting points from which I could attribute particular conversations to Beara. My analysis testifies to this effect because my conclusions are often phrased to the effect that there is nothing to link Mr. Beara to a particular transcript. In other words, it is obvious that I became privy to the OTP opinion much later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good, thank you. Sir, yesterday my learned colleague was asking you about the word "burazer" and "buraz" on page 40, line 20, of yesterday's transcript, and he read part of your report on page 17, and I objected, and it was, you know, overruled. But let me turn to page 17 of your report, and help me on that category. It's actually under the first intercept if you are following along, which is section -- it says 11 as printed. That might be a typographical error, but it is during the text of your discussion of the first intercept, 13th July, 1995, at 1009 hours. Now, when you discussed "sjor" and "gospon" and "burazer" in that paragraph, I thought - and I want to keep it in context - if you could focus for us and have it -- and read for us the paragraph before that where you discuss the very word that my learned friend was trying to challenge you on as to whether or not it's a western or eastern or Dalmatian or predominantly Croatian or Cakavian word. You give us that immediately prior to that, do you not, sir? Do you see that in your report? Where you discuss the word "burazer."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Sjor" is a dialect-marked word. It is a feature of coastal regions. "Burazer," however, covers a broad area, and we hear this every day on TV, in various shows. I can hear it in my conversations with my own brother. Two days ago he called me and addressed me by calling me "burazer." I told you yesterday that my head of the Academy of Sciences and Arts called me "burazer" hundreds of times. "Burazer" is a common word. There's also a truncated form, "buraz." Both are of Turkish origin. "Buraz" is somewhat more often used in Bosnia than in Serbia, but this word is not a cornerstone around which any house can be built. This is just a lexical feature.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Professor, help me with this. Can you share with us the difference between a variant and a dialect?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This concerns the Serbo-Croatian standard language, which used to have two variants from the very beginning, the eastern and the western or the Belgrade and the Zagreb variants respectively, the Ekavian or the Ijekavian variants. However, in practice in real conversations, the latter is Ijekavian, and everybody including my kind hostesses here in the Tribunal, when they point me to the "lijevo," I immediately know where they come from, where they went to school, and where their education in Serbo-Croatian comes from. The variants differ the most in terminology, in the lexic or the words. The Croats as a rule translated foreign words that infiltrated; the Serbs did not, however. In Serbia, we have schnitzels, and in Zagreb they have steaks. In Serbia, we play football, and in Zagreb they play the same game but under a Croatian name. These are variants at the level of the standard language, whereas dialects are a different thing. We have three dialects, and within these dialects that are subdivisions into various speeches, colloquialisms, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: When you say "knjizevni," is that not scholarly and one is, like, a common discussion because my learned friend from the OTP yesterday even told you at page 41 at lines 10 through 14 when he was describing his pattern of speech, he says: "I'm an English-speaking person, and I use the word 'man' quite frequently in my speech." Although we haven't heard it in his questions today, I think when we scholarly -- or yesterday, when we scholarly speak or as you say, "knjizevni," we may have a different variant from when we speak in our normal conversational pattern of speech. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the linguistic norm or the standard language is a necessity in anyone's society. For a community to function to pass and implement important decisions, such a community must have a linguistic norm or a code which is known as the standard language. A linguistic norm in my terminology, which I often convey to my students during my lectures, is a functional violation of a language. A language has to have a norm that is used in official documents. For example, judgements have to be passed in a standard language which is received pronunciation in any state. There's also another thing, which is colloquial language, the language of everyday conversations in everyday life, and this is the so-called substandard speech. The standard form of a language is coloured or peppered with the elements of local dialects. A judgement in Belgrade, for example, in Novi Sad, or in Nis must be issued and printed in the same standard language, and the judges who serve in these three cities will use their substandard language, the languages of their own region when they speak. The basis of those substandard languages is the standard language, but it is coloured by some dialectal influences, and that's how things are all over the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. Just looking at this table here, we see that you analysed four intercepts on -- well, relating to the 13th of July, and we talked about the one at 1009 hours where it purports to be that the person said "Beara speaking," and we saw the B/C/S version where the word speaking or "govorim" doesn't appear. But with respect to these four on the 13th, and let me just try to capture this for you, we know the very next intercept - and I think the Prosecution takes the similar position - they're not even claiming it's Mr. Beara. It's another fact that they are, for whatever reason unimportant to you, trying to tie in with our case, so we know that one is insignificant, at least for your expertise and purposes. The next one at 1945 on the 13th of July, the Prosecution has taken a position that it is not Ljubisa Beara, so that's not related to Mr. Beara, although the name "Ljubisa" appears on it as we've identified three times. The very next one, the Prosecution -- although I thought I had it correct, the Prosecution now is taking the position that it is uncertain who the Ljubisa is, so they can't even tell us whether it's Ljubisa Beara. So out of the four on the 13th, only one is that the Prosecution is alleging is against Mr. Beara, and we discussed that. My question goes to the very next intercept, however, the 14th of July, which is one intercept at 2102 hours. Now, I wants to show you something that I didn't have a copy of, and that's the actual intercept when the intercept operator was here who captured that conversation, and he helped us out by identifying various marks or changes that he made in his handwritten notes or manuscript, as you call it, of this purported conversation. Now, if we could please have for you, Mr. Remetic, PIC 40 and also PIC 41, and it's split up into two pages, so forgive me for that, but I think the main one we'll look at is PIC 41, but let's look at both in -- for purposes of completeness because the Prosecution didn't show you that, but they had a couple of questions on this intercept. But let's see -- because you didn't read it -- their testimony, I want you to see what he circled in terms of changes or alterations that he may have made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object to this line of inquiry. It is true that I did cross-examine the witness with respect to this particular intercept, but the question that was put to him was to identify the error that he indicated in his report and nothing beyond that. So I think this is well beyond the scope of cross-examination as concerns this particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does the witness understand English? I would imagine he does.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: A little bit I think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah. I would imagine I would prefer to discuss this in his absence. Let me consult with my colleagues anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's true that possibly does fall within the parameters of a redirect, but on the other hand we believe that this witness is not in a position to add anything to what we've heard already, so we suggest you move to your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, after now looking at this 14th and the one intercepted on the 14th, and we will go back to your table, if possible - I know we just switched from it - which is appendix 1. I know you have several of the markings with respect to the three intercepts for the 15th and then one other one. Now, you fairly and objectively place on the two intercepts the 15th of July, 955 and 957. You put a positive sign for "participant revealed himself or was revealed as Beara," correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN REMETIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the operator, two of them actually said that he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you're not taking any -- or you are not suggesting or trying to determine whether the operators were truthful or honest or mistaken. You just simply said the -- and you took their word for it, correct, and therefore you put a positive sign with respect to those two at 955 and 957? Wait, wait.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I object to the question. It is leading, and I would ask my colleague to rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because we were doing something else at the time. Yes, it is leading. Definitely, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you just tell us how you came up with the conclusion which rendered the opinion that you place a positive sign on this first category for the intercepts at 955 and 957 of the 15th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's hear what Mr. Vanderpuye has to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, this was asked and answered already on direct, and I don't think it's appropriate at this stage in redirect examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's come to an end, please, Mr. Ostojic. Let's conclude.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is he allowed to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, of course. No, no, of course. You proceed with your next question. It has been suggested by Mr. Vanderpuye this question has already been answered.
